title: The wells of Badr
hookLine: a small, outnumbered band of Muslims meets the Meccan army by the wells of Badr, and wins

cards: That same first Ramadan, word comes: a large army has marched out of Mecca, the city that drove them out. About a thousand men, with horses and armor.

The Muslims who ride out to meet them number a little over three hundred. The biographers say they have two horses between them and about seventy camels, taking turns riding. Some have no armor at all.
They camp near a group of wells in a valley called Badr, on the caravan road southwest of Medina. The night before, it rains. In the morning, the two sides face each other across the sand.

teach.b: Two moments before the battle are worth knowing. The first is about the wells, from the early biographer Ibn Ishaq. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ stopped the army at one spot.
A companion, al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir, asked politely: is this place one God has shown you, or your own judgment, a matter of war and planning? His own judgment, the Prophet said.
Then, said al-Hubab, this isn't the right place.
Let's move to the well nearest the enemy, build a cistern, and keep the water on our side. And the Prophet said: you've given good advice, and moved the whole army.
A prophet, taking correction from a soldier, in front of everyone. The second moment is the night.
Sahih Muslim describes the Prophet standing in prayer, hands raised, calling on God so long and so hard that his cloak slipped off his shoulders.
Abu Bakr put it back and told him: enough, God will keep his promise to you. Then the battle. The Meccans broke.

Sahih al-Bukhari counts seventy of them killed and seventy taken captive, among the dead several of the leaders who had tormented the Muslims in Mecca. The biographers name about fourteen Muslims who died.

teach.h: WHEN YOU WERE WEAK AND FEW.
teach.b: The Qur'an looks back: God had already helped you at Badr, when you were weak and few.
It says the Muslims were strengthened with angels, and that the victory was God's, not theirs.
Muslim teachers often tell Badr not as a story about strength, but the opposite: how little they had, and how much came through anyway.

how: Some Muslims mark the battle of Badr in Ramadan with talks in mosques about the people who took part, whom later generations honored as the people of Badr.

o: a desert fort where Medina stored its grain
a valley of wells where an outnumbered few won
a market town where traders sold spices

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Prophet refused advice about where to camp
he asked if it was his judgment or revelation, then moved the army on al-Hubab's advice.
the Qur'an says the Muslims were weak at Badr
God helped you at Badr, when you were weak and few.
the Muslims had more horses than the Meccans
the biographers say about two horses and seventy camels, taking turns.

games.q: you're a companion. the Prophet has chosen a spot for the army, but you think it's a bad one. what do you do?
o: ask if it's revelation or his own judgment, then advise.
move your own tent without telling anyone.
games.why: al-Hubab asked, heard it was the Prophet's judgment, and advised the nearest well. the Prophet said: good advice, and moved everyone.

practice: Go back to a time in your own life when the odds were against you, not enough money, time or strength, and somehow you got through: a stranger's help, a door that opened at the last minute.
Let it come back in detail, where you were and what you felt, and notice how little you actually had. If you pray, you can thank God for it.

wordCard.voice: Badr, the valley where a small, outnumbered band of Muslims met the Meccan army in the first Ramadan, and won.

orig.note: Arabic: Badr, the valley and its wells. the word also means a full moon.

carryVoice: Your line: few against many. Two horses, seventy camels, three hundred and some. That's day two hundred sixty-four.
